Aerospace engineering is a beast.
Maybe the last field of engineering that covers multiple huge topics like aerodynamics, 
astrodynamics, GNC, propulsion and all the advanced engineering mathematics.
This is overwhelming.
The solution is to find the topicsc that suits you and gives enough hapiness, success and 
passion to keep you going.
I think there is no other way to achieve something in this field.
After almost a year long reading and investigating aerospace engineering as a field of science I 
think I have found my topics.

Aerodynamics, astrodymanics and GNC.
If I define the problem space covered by them I get the "atmospheric re-entry",
"satellites/megaconstellations on Low Stellar Body Orbit" and "spacecraft
landing". Beside these industry reality - serious - topics there are the childish dreams
like being able model any - including chaotic ones like human communication -
phenomea mathematically with the cunning topic of psychohistory, and the "dogfight in space".
I can have dreams, haven't I?

# Aerodynamics

This is where the story starts. The young teenager of me reading a monthly
journal - called Top Gun - about fighter jets and military technology. 
There was an article about the development of the F-18 Hornet and the
fact that mentioned its wing designed by mathematical models. I clearly remember
that I asked the question "how"? This question found me many times in the last
30 years in many forms. When I learned software engineering the one of the main
questions, a bit silly one but with infinite motivation, was what computer
science resource (code, cpu, memory, etc) is needed to model airflows and
turbulence. On this fertile ground landed the Theodore von Karman biography.
Unfortunately the biography doesn't detail the modeling part, but it is still
the book I open when I need a boost.

In the last year I read the "Boyd" book about Colonel Boyd who is the father of
the OODA loop and the F-15/16/18 planes with his energy-efficient-theory that is
based on thermodynamics and foundational approach in modern dogfighting. For me,
this is where mechanical sympathy builds a bridge between the physical world and
numbers and provide control. Hardcore engineering. It makes me shiver, to be
honest.

There is another factor why aerodynamics teasing me: it is one of the most
difficult engineering field.

The daydreamer part of me wants hobby project where I build the "fighter jet of
my dreams" or running a local CFD model on the F-15/F-16 model I have and
building mechanical sympathy with the plane. 

# Astrodynamics

The most interesting part in a science-fiction movie for me is flying in space.
How does it work? What are the rules one has to consider? I want enough
information to imagine when the hull of a spaceship start rattling during
landing and why. I want to feel it. Yes, mechanical sympathy again.

And two event occured in close proximity: 

- the Expanse series landed with its high fidelity space operations
- Elite: Dangerous game was released with its "Flight Assist Off" flying mode
  that simulates real physics

I did not notice, but my mind was screaming for answers for the whats and hows.
This screaming for answers has the "dogfight in space" idea in my mind.

From a serious, space industry point of view, astrodynamics is about "how do we
get there" which is pretty neat even though it draws strict limits around the
space opera in my mind.

# GNC

Seemingly the most boring topic from the three, but actually it is at the centre
of everything. It is the essence of engineering mathematics: control. "What
input do I have to provide to achieve this and that output?" It is about
feedback and even though sounds very boring this is an extremely interesting
field. I mentioned mechanical sympathy a few times above. GNC is The Mechanical
Sympathy. It expects you to understand a system to its core so intimately you
can identify the least needed intput to make the system behave as you wish. In
other words, you are The Master of Puppets and The Man Behind the Curtain, and
there is no evil plan. This is the point where Mathematics enter the game and
says: "Dynamical Systems". Control is a, using the already known stable points
effectively and, b, finding new stable points in a chaotic system and build up
the structure of control. This is the reason I want to be able to model anything
mathematically.

This is my master plan.

All of the three topics will get its own blog entry where I am going to clarify
further the possible areas. For this clarification process I'll use AI tools
because they are really good in summaries and overviewing a huge volume of
literature and giving me pointers. The output of the research is going to be
description of the topics and available papers and textbooks in the partical
segment.
